questiontext.text:
Butterfly populations along a transect

An ecologist organised butterfly surveys at 22 monitoring sites at different distances from a nature reserve.

Download the dataset. It contains four columns:

  • Site: the monitoring-site identifier.
  • Distance_km: distance from the nature reserve, in kilometres.
  • Butterfly_count: the number of butterflies recorded.
  • Survey_status: whether the survey was completed.

The field team recorded a blank in the count column when no butterflies were observed during a completed survey.

Download butterflies_data.csv

Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient between distance from the nature reserve and butterfly count.

Give your answer to three decimal places.

\(r=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution: The missing butterflies

1. What do the missing values mean?

Before calculating a correlation coefficient, we need to understand why some butterfly counts are recorded as NA.

The survey status shows that every survey was completed. The field team's recording convention explains that NA in a completed survey means that no butterflies were observed.

For this particular dataset, those missing counts should therefore be replaced with zero.

Why does the correlation change?

By omitting the NA rows, we excluded every site where no butterflies were observed.

The remaining observations showed an increasing trend, but they did not represent the complete survey.

Including the zero counts changes the relationship substantially. The apparent positive correlation becomes a negative correlation.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text:
Correct! Replacing the NA values with zero, in accordance with the survey's recording convention, allows us to include all 20 sites.

This indicates a strong negative linear relationship between distance from the nature reserve and butterfly count.

Note however that the complete scatterplot reveals a very different pattern.

● Green: completed surveys where NA represents zero butterflies.

The complete dataset shows that butterflies were absent at the more distant monitoring sites.

This is important to handle correctly. If you omitted the NA rows, you would get a very different looking plot, correlation, and draw different conclusions

The resulting Pearson correlation coefficient would be \(r={@r_omitted_display@}\), suggesting a weak positive linear relationship: butterfly counts tend to increase with distance from the nature reserve, although the observations are quite scattered.

Those sites were surveyed, and zero butterflies were observed there.

Key lesson: Not all NA values mean the same thing

In this dataset, NA has two different meanings:

  • Completed survey: NA means no butterflies were observed, so the count is zero.
  • Not completed: NA means the count is unknown. It must not be replaced with zero.

The two uncompleted surveys should retain their NA values in the cleaned dataset. They cannot be included in the Pearson correlation calculation because their butterfly counts are unknown.

Neither deleting every NA row nor replacing every NA with zero is appropriate here.

Always investigate why data are missing before deciding how to handle them.

Your coefficient matches the result obtained when every row containing NA is deleted. However, some of these surveys were completed. Check the recording convention to determine what NA means in those cases.

If we exclude every row containing NA, we retain only the sites where a numerical butterfly count was recorded.

The resulting Pearson correlation coefficient is \(r={@r_omitted_display@}\).

This suggests a weak positive linear relationship: butterfly counts tend to increase with distance from the nature reserve, although the observations are quite scattered.

The scatterplot shows why.

falsefeedback.text: Your correlation coefficient is not correct. Check which observations you included and how you handled the NA values.

truefeedback.text:
Your coefficient matches the result obtained when every NA is replaced with zero.

But two surveys were not completed. Their butterfly counts are unknown: we cannot assume that no butterflies would have been observed.

Use the survey status to distinguish genuine zero counts from genuinely missing observations.

The following scatterplot incorrectly places those two sites on the horizontal axis.
